w:r.w:t: LAVA: A Lightweight Benchmarking Framework for Robust and Efficient Deepfake Voice Detection
University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City (UEH), Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam

Deepfake voice detectors are difficult to compare across incompatible data partitions, score conventions, calibration, preprocessing, and timing. LAVA applies common artifact-integrity, P(FAKE), diagnostic-stress, and runtime contracts while preserving native computation. We evaluate four locally trained Mel-sequence artifacts and externally pretrained RawNet2 and AASIST reference artifacts, whose training and calibration provenance differs. SHA-256 grouping quarantined 30 cross-label files and produced a checksum-group-disjoint manifest; clean evaluation used all 2,737 test recordings. ShuffleNetV2 achieved the highest AUC (0.9929) and lowest EER (1.46%); its threshold-specific F1 was 0.9824. On one single-thread desktop CPU, MobileNetV3 had the lowest end-to-end latency (43.81 ms; RTF 0.0146), while ShuffleNetV2 required 62.52 ms (RTF 0.0208). A fixed stratified 100-recording diagnostic evaluated seeded AWGN, four codec round trips, and simulated replay. On this subset, low-SNR noise was the main observed weakness, and ShuffleNetV2 retained the highest mean stressed F1 (0.8133). Using diagnostic-subset EER, mean stressed F1, and end-to-end RTF, the exploratory analysis identifies MobileNetV3 and ShuffleNetV2 as non-dominated under the evaluated objectives. These findings support deployment-oriented offline comparison, but do not establish full-test robustness, unseen-corpus generalization, physical-replay robustness, streaming, edge-device performance, or multi-seed stability.

w:r.w:t: , comparisons remain difficult because studies differ in data partitions, label conventions, input duration, preprocessing, calibration, and runtime boundaries. Byte-identical recordings across data splits introduce an additional integrity concern.

LAVA compares heterogeneous deployed artifacts through one interface while preserving their Mel-sequence or raw-waveform pipelines. It standardizes integrity checks, P(FAKE) semantics, stress conditions, outputs, and timing. Four artifacts were trained locally; RawNet2 and AASIST are external references. Clean evaluation uses the full test set, stress diagnostics use a fixed subset, and timing uses one desktop CPU, so the evidence does not establish general robustness, streaming, or edge-device operation. The study addresses:
RQ1: How do deployed artifacts compare on clean AUC and EER, and how should threshold-dependent metrics be interpreted under heterogeneous training and calibration?
RQ2: How does absolute performance change under the executed noise, codec, and simulated-replay conditions on the fixed diagnostic subset?
RQ3: Which artifacts are non-dominated across diagnostic-subset EER, mean stressed F1, and end-to-end RTF?

LAVA contributes: (1) checksum-group-disjoint, artifact-traceable clean evaluation centered on AUC/EER and provenance; (2) matched fixed-subset diagnostics for noise, compression, and simulated replay with aggregate failure-pattern analysis; and (3) desktop-CPU timing and exploratory three-objective Pareto analysis for scenario-specific recommendations.

The surveyed studies assess clean discrimination, robustness or generalization, and efficiency under different protocols, making deployment-oriented comparison across heterogeneous artifacts difficult. LAVA applies one artifact-traceable offline contract to six available artifacts. It does not claim unseen-corpus generalization, physical-replay robustness, streaming, or edge-device validation.

LAVA separates canonical data and integrity (D), registered detectors (M), conditions (C), measurements (E), and analyses (A). The registry records each artifact's input, duration, threshold, and provenance; adapters preserve native computation while exposing common scores and resource measures. Runners derive statistics and figures from
stored sample-level outputs while distinguishing planned from executed conditions (Figures 1 and 2).

Evidence is limited by heterogeneous training and calibration, a fixed 100-recording diagnostic subset, simulated rather than physical replay, and one desktop CPU. The dataset cannot establish speaker, source, generator, parent-recording, or cross-dataset independence. No unseen-corpus, edge-device, streaming, or multi-seed evaluation was conducted; RSS is whole-process memory, EfficientNet-B0 is an available warm-up checkpoint, and paired scores for sample-level prediction-flip analysis are unavailable.

Recommendations remain artifact-, objective-, and platform-specific. Under the evaluated objectives, ShuffleNetV2 is the stronger predictive-performance candidate: it achieved the highest clean AUC, lowest clean EER, highest mean stressed F1, and remained non-dominated at RTF 0.0208. MobileNetV3 is the lower-latency candidate on the measured host. These findings do not identify a universally optimal model or rank architectures independently of their available artifacts.

LAVA provides an evidence-traceable comparison of six heterogeneous voice anti-spoofing artifacts. Under the evaluated conditions, MobileNetV3 and ShuffleNetV2 are non-dominated, while low-SNR noise is the main weakness observed on the fixed diagnostic subset. Future work should retain paired scores and test the full set, unseen corpora, physical replay, streaming, and target edge hardware
